edaphos

From Greek ἔδαφος — “soil, ground.”

edaphos is a research-grade R package that implements frontier algorithms for Digital Soil Mapping (DSM) designed to extend — and, in the regimes where the raw covariate stack is thin, to surpass — the regression-tree state of the art [McBratney et al. 2003; Wadoux et al. 2020]. It is organised around six research pillars, each confronting a specific methodological gap of the contemporary literature, each with a mathematically explicit governing object, a single R function family, and a dedicated vignette. v1.7.0 closes the circle with a capstone cross-pillar vignette that integrates the pillars in a single Cerrado sampling-campaign narrative causally grounded in the generative DSM framework of Zhang and Wadoux 2026.

Correlation → Causation · Black-box ML → Physics-Informed ML
Static maps → 4D forecasts · Labelled-only → Foundation models
Fixed sampling → Autonomous Active Learning · Classical kernels → Quantum kernels

Why edaphos exists: the scientific gap

Zhang and Wadoux (2026) ask a deceptively simple question: Can Digital Soil Mapping Be Causal? Their answer:

“In principle, yes — but only if the DSM model specifies the mechanisms and processes that link soil-forming factors to soil properties, rather than relying on associations themselves.”

They identify three conditions that must be met for causal inference from observational data (and soil surveys are almost always observational):

  1. An explicit causal model — a DAG over the variables of interest.
  2. Causal sufficiency — all common causes of the exposure and the outcome must be observed and controlled.
  3. Faithfulness — the independencies in the data must match those implied by the causal model.

And they distinguish two competing views of causality:

View Lógica central Challenge in DSM
Successionist Regularities / repeatable associations ⇒ causal claim Simpson’s paradox; spurious associations; no temporal sequencing
Generative Soil-forming factors act through explicit processes that produce soil properties Requires process-informed models; directly satisfies condition 1

Each of edaphos’s ten pillars addresses one of these gaps with a concrete, reproducible computational machinery, with quantified uncertainty at every step.

It is worth being precise about how far that goes. The generative paradigm asks for models in which soil properties arise from explicitly specified processes. Pillar 2 does that for the depth dimension, and piml_profile_fit_mechanistic() derives its equation from a carbon balance. Pillar 1’s graph, however, is over observed state variables — climate, terrain, texture — not over process parameters, and the shipped graph is rejected by causal_dag_test() on 33 of the 37 conditional independencies it implies (28 of 37 after removing spatial structure). So the package operationalises pieces of the generative paradigm and gives you the tools to find out where they fail; it does not deliver it end-to-end, and the failures are reported rather than hidden.

🆕 v1.7.0 — capstone cross-pillar vignette

The headline feature of the current release is a new vignette: “Uma decisão de amostragem sob incerteza no Cerrado” (vignette("capstone-cerrado-campaign")). It answers a single question with the pillars acting together:

A team has budget for exactly eight new soil-sampling points in the Cerrado. Where should they go — and why?

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant LIT as Literature
    participant P1 as P1 Causal
    participant P2 as P2 PIML
    participant P3 as P3 4D
    participant P4 as P4 Foundation
    participant P5 as P5 AL
    participant P6 as P6 Quantum
    participant DEC as Decision

    LIT->>P1: Gemma 4 extracts causal edges
    P1->>P1: Backdoor adjustment on DAG
    P1->>P2: Identify exposures (MAP, cover, clay)
    P2->>P2: Fit pedogenetic ODE (MCMC)
    P2->>P5: Physics gate -- exclude implausible sites
    P3->>P5: Kalman gain priorities
    P4->>P5: Encoder embeddings (128D)
    P5->>P5: Greedy hybrid selection
    P5->>P6: Q-KRR second opinion
    P6->>DEC: Epistemic + aleatoric SD
    DEC->>DEC: Weighted final score
    Note over DEC: 8 sites with CI-explicit ranking

The vignette produces a weighted decision matrix integrating:

  • Pillar 1 causal-effect posteriors (block-bootstrap in k-means clusters).
  • Pillar 2 pedogenetic ODE posteriors (k1,k2,σk_1, k_2, \sigma).
  • Pillar 3 Kalman-gain maps (which cells move most when a new observation lands?).
  • Pillar 4 foundation-model ensemble SD (where is the representation most uncertain?).
  • Pillar 5 QRF prediction-interval width + cLHS diversity.
  • Pillar 6 Q-KRR epistemic SD (a GP-equivalent second opinion).

The output is a ranked table of eight sampling locations, each with an explicit causal justification tied back to the Zhang & Wadoux (2026) framework.

📖 Build the vignette:

vignette("capstone-cerrado-campaign", package = "edaphos")

🆕 v2.7.0 – v2.8.0 — Torch autograd ports + honest head-to-head WoSIS benchmark

Two new releases complete the v2.x arc:

v2.7.0 — Torch autograd backends for Pilares 8, 9 and 10. Replaces the ELM-style (hidden layers frozen, gradient only on the head) pure-R fits with full-backprop torch::optim_adam training. Each *_fit() gains backend = c("r", "torch") and device = c("cpu", "mps", "cuda"); pure-R remains the default fallback for users without libtorch. A proper 2-D conditional U-Net replaces the MLP denoiser in DDPM, and the GAT layer uses torch::index_add scatter for softmax-per-source attention.

Cross-pillar head-to-head on 1 095 WoSIS profiles. Five spatially blocked folds, log1p(SOC), scored against the achievable null — predicting each fold’s training-fold mean, not the global mean, which would be an oracle over the very rows being scored:

Method RMSE R² vs global mean NSE vs training-fold mean draws
P1 OLS (DAG-selected covariates) 0.586 +0.162 +0.204 300
P5 QRF 0.597 +0.131 +0.174 99
P7 BHS 0.613 +0.084 +0.130 200
P4 Foundation embeddings + QRF 0.618 +0.070 +0.117 99
P6 Quantum KRR 0.663 −0.073 −0.019 100
P10 GAT (trained attention) 0.672 −0.101 −0.046 8

RMSE is in log1p(g/kg) and is not comparable to a g/kg figure. The draws column is the ensemble each method actually got: they are not equal, and a ranking that ignores that is comparing budgets.

These folds carry a 68 km buffer: training rows within that distance of any test row are discarded, which cost 88 training rows across the five folds — 2.0% of the fold-wise training rows, not of the 1,095 profiles — and raised the realised minimum training-to-test distance from 15.2 km to 68.5 km on these 1,095 profiles. (12.3 km is the corresponding figure for the denser 3,077-profile causal extract, a different data set; earlier versions of this README quoted it here by mistake.) Blocking without a dead zone under-states generalisation error (Roberts et al. 2017), and 15.2 km sits well inside the 69 km range at which the one fitted depth-function parameter with an identified variogram is still correlated. (Earlier versions said “the 55–68 km range” from two identified parameters; those variograms were computed on Gaussian-likelihood fits. Under the lognormal likelihood the package now defaults to, only one of the four parameters has an identified range — see data-raw/piml_parameter_variograms.R.)

What the buffer is worth, measured rather than asserted. Earlier versions of this README stated that P10 GAT “went from RMSE 0.617 to 0.679 … dropping from fifth to last”. That comparison was made by hand, was never scripted, and does not reproduce: it also predated the correction of the Pillar-10 graph from Euclidean degrees to great-circle kilometres, so it compared two different models. data-raw/buffer_effect.R now runs the same harness with the buffer switched off and writes inst/extdata/buffer_effect.rds. Fold-mean RMSE, five methods on identical test blocks:

Method unbuffered buffered Δ rank un. rank buf.
P1 OLS (DAG-selected covariates) 0.583 0.583 +0.000 1 1
P5 QRF 0.588 0.592 +0.004 2 2
P7 BHS 0.605 0.608 +0.003 3 3
P6 Quantum KRR 0.660 0.663 +0.003 4 4
P10 GAT (trained attention) 0.672 0.680 +0.007 5 5

The buffer costs every method a little and the graph network the most, which is the direction the mechanism predicts — a network built on a spatial neighbour graph is what gains most from training points immediately across a block boundary. But the effect is an order of magnitude smaller than previously reported and the ranking is identical either way. The buffer stays because it is the right protocol, not because it changes the answer. (P4 is scored in a separate harness and is absent from this comparison rather than omitted quietly.)

The honest reading. Ordinary least squares on a DAG-selected covariate subset is the strongest method here. None of the five more elaborate pillars beats it on this task, and the spread between the top four is small relative to the fold-to-fold variation. Two methods fall below the achievable null — P6 and, once the fold buffer is in place, P10.

Note which null. The third column is skill against the mean of each fold’s training rows, the null a deployed map could use. The second is against the global mean, which is computed partly from the rows being scored. The conventional per-fold R-squared uses a third and stricter denominator still — the test fold’s own mean — and by that measure three methods score negative. The manuscript reported that third figure under the first’s name until edaphos_nse(), which requires the null as an argument, made the three impossible to conflate.

Two figures for P10, both correct. The +0.112 above is a fixed-configuration comparison with every pillar at its defaults. Under nested cross-validation with tuned hyperparameters and a 10-member ensemble, the same GAT reaches NSE +0.184 against a tuned QRF’s +0.165 (difference +0.019, 95 % block-bootstrap CI [−0.021, +0.057], P(GAT ahead) = 0.844 — a consistent edge, not a significant one). Those answer different questions: “how do the pillars compare out of the box” versus “does a tuned GAT beat a tuned forest”. Runner: data-raw/pilar10_gat_tuning.R; bundle inst/extdata/pilar10_gat_tuning.rds.

The torch backend, fixed. An earlier backend = "torch" GAT trained a linear head end-to-end with no input skip and no early stopping, and scored NSE ≈ −0.40 — worse than predicting the mean — on held-out Cerrado nodes. Porting the R backend’s readout skip and best-validation selection into it lifts it to NSE ≈ 0.52 across four 20 %-held-out splits (OLS 0.55, R-GAT 0.54 on the same splits): competitive, not superior. The default backend stays "r" — marginally better here and dependency-free — while "torch" is now a correct, non-degenerate alternative rather than a broken one.

Earlier releases published a different table — RMSE ≈ 14.1 g/kg and R² of 0.034 / 0.064 / 0.070 for P4 / P5 / P7, described as a three-way tie. Those figures came from the raw g/kg scale, where 11 profiles (1 % of n) carry 48 % of the total sum of squares, and from an R² clamped at zero that hid negative values in 21 of 30 method-fold cells. The P4 row was additionally computed over a raster of stats::rnorm() noise. They have been withdrawn. tests/testthat/test-headline-claims.R now binds every figure in this section to the shipped bundle.

Runners: data-raw/benchmark_wosis_p4_p5_p7.R and data-raw/benchmark_wosis_6pilar.R; bundle inst/extdata/benchmark_wosis_6pilar.rds.

Provenance. The WoSIS profiles were sampled between 1960 and 2010 (median 1982); the covariates are present-day products (SoilGrids 2020, WorldClim 2.1, SRTM 2000, WorldCover 2020). Land cover is measured roughly four decades after the median observation, so part of the irreducible error is temporal mismatch rather than model inadequacy.

Version Scope

Two bridges shipped alongside (v2.1.1 + v2.1.2)

Pilar 1 × Pilar 5 — Causal Active Learning. al_query_causal() picks the next sample(s) that most reduce the variance of a specific causal effect (not the generic predictive variance of classical AL). Closed-form leverage heuristic + optional bootstrap-exact mode.

Pilar 3 × Pilar 5 — Temporal Active Learning with EnKF feedback. al_query_temporal() ranks candidate cells by their Kalman-gain norm after the latest assimilation step, with three combine modes (gain, gain × SD, percentile-normalised).

Scaffolds for v2.2.0 → v2.8.0

Each scaffold file includes the full scientific motivation, architecture plan and TODO checklist.

Installation 

# Core package (light: clhs + httr2 + jsonlite + ranger + stats)
remotes::install_github("HugoMachadoRodrigues/edaphos",
                         build_vignettes = TRUE)

# Optional heavy dependencies (Pillars 2 Neural ODE, 3, 4)
install.packages("torch");      torch::install_torch()

# Optional lightweight extras
install.packages("dagitty")       # Pillar 1 DAGs
install.packages("bnlearn")       # Pillar 1 structure learning
install.packages("dbarts")        # Pillar 1 BART estimator
install.packages("aqp")           # Pillar 2 example pedons
install.packages("terra")         # Pillar 3 / 4 raster stacks
install.packages("geodata")       # Pillar 5 live SoilGrids fetch

# Pillar 1 LLM backend (one of the three)
#  (a) LOCAL, recommended: Ollama + Gemma 4
#       https://ollama.com
#       ollama pull gemma4:latest
#  (b) OpenAI:       Sys.setenv(OPENAI_API_KEY = "...")
#  (c) Anthropic:    Sys.setenv(ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = "...")

# Pillar 6 optional quantum backend
install.packages("reticulate")    # for qiskit / qiskit-nature / PySCF bridge

The package imports only six CRAN packages for its core functionality; every heavier stack is opt-in via Suggests and is required only by the pillar that uses it. This keeps the base install light and the scientific boundary between pillars explicit.

🔗 Unified uncertainty API uncertainty_* ✅ v1.6.0 edaphos_posterior S3 class + uncertainty_calibrate() returning CRPS / PICP / MPIW / reliability diagram. 7 of the 10 pillars carry an as_edaphos_posterior() method (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7); pillars 8, 9 and 10 do not — see the note below
🎬 Capstone vignette — ✅ v1.7.0 “Uma decisão de amostragem sob incerteza no Cerrado” — integrating the six pillars that existed at v1.7.0, causally grounded in Zhang & Wadoux (2026)

Which pillars reach the uncertainty API, and why three do not. methods("as_edaphos_posterior") returns 12 methods covering pillars 1 through 7. Pillars 8 (neural operators), 9 (diffusion) and 10 (graph attention) have none, and this row previously claimed “every pillar”.

For pillar 10 the omission is deliberate rather than pending. A fitted GAT exposes only member_sd, the spread between ensemble members that differ in their random seed. That is not a predictive distribution: it measures initialisation variance, and the function’s own documentation concedes that a ±1.96·sd band covers about a quarter of the profiles. Wrapping it in edaphos_posterior() would make a calibration number computable and meaningless. The benchmark instead builds an interval explicitly, as member spread plus a noise term whose scale is estimated by inner spatially blocked CV, and reports it as such (benchmark_fit_p10_gat()). Even so, that interval carries no information about extrapolation distance — see data-raw/interval_width_vs_extrapolation.R, where its width correlates −0.08 with distance to the nearest training profile while its error correlates +0.11.

Pillars 8 and 9 return field-valued objects (operator outputs, map patches), for which a per-site scalar posterior is the wrong shape; they are evaluated by their own task-appropriate diagnostics instead.

Every pillar ships with (i) a mathematically explicit governing object; (ii) an R function family; (iii) one or more vignettes deriving the object from first principles and demonstrating it on real or reproducible synthetic data; and (iv) a @references entry in the shared vignettes/references.bib.

Pillar 1 — Causal inference on a pedogenetic graph

Motivation

The OLS lm(soc ~ ndvi) that every DSM pipeline runs implicitly reports the total association, which inflates the direct NDVI → SOC effect with every backdoor path through shared ancestors (topography, precipitation, vegetation cover). Pillar 1 exposes this using Pearl’s structural-causal-model apparatus [Pearl 2009].

Governing object

Given a pedogenetic Directed Acyclic Graph G=(V,E)G = (V, E), the backdoor-adjusted direct effect of exposure XX on outcome YY is

βx→ydo=∂𝔼[Y∣X=x,Z=z]∂x,Z∈𝚍𝚊𝚐𝚒𝚝𝚝𝚢::𝚊𝚍𝚓𝚞𝚜𝚝𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝𝚂𝚎𝚝𝚜(G,X,Y). \beta_{x\to y}^{\text{do}} \;=\; \frac{\partial\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[Y \mid X=x,\, Z=z\bigr]}{\partial x}, \qquad Z \;\in\; \texttt{dagitty::adjustmentSets}(G,X,Y).

Classical API 

library(edaphos)
data(br_cerrado)

g   <- causal_cerrado_dag()
adj <- causal_adjustment_set(g, exposure = "ndvi", outcome = "soc")
adj
#> [1] "map_mm" "slope"  "twi"

fit <- causal_estimate_effect(
  br_cerrado, g,
  exposure = "ndvi", outcome = "soc",
  effect   = "direct"
)
fit
#> <edaphos_causal_effect>
#>   ndvi -> soc
#>   adjustment set : {map_mm, slope, twi}
#>   direct effect  : 18.43   (95% CI: 14.61, 22.25)
#>   naive effect   : 49.36   (un-adjusted, likely confounded)

The naive OLS over-reports NDVI’s effect on SOC by ~2.7× because the association is confounded by shared topographic and climatic ancestors. Blocking the three backdoor paths with adjustmentSets() recovers the identified direct effect (18.4, 95% CI [14.6, 22.3]).

🤖 From expert DAGs to LLM-driven Knowledge Graphs

The central scientific bottleneck of causal DSM is DAG construction. Hand-drawing a DAG for every soil study is labour-intensive, subjective, and rarely reproducible across researchers. Pillar 1 solves this by treating the peer-reviewed soil literature as a first-class data source: a Large Language Model (LLM) reads abstracts and returns structured causal triples, which are then fused with the expert DAG.

This machinery directly operationalises condition 1 of Zhang & Wadoux (2026) — “an explicit causal model” — at the scale of the literature instead of the individual expert.

Why Gemma 4?

As of v1.5.0 the default LLM backend is Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, served locally through Ollama. Four properties made Gemma 4 the right choice for causal-KG extraction in pedology:

  1. Scientific reasoning competence. Gemma 4 inherits the instruction-tuned reasoning of the Gemma family and performs well on benchmarks involving multi-hop causal language (MMLU “social-sciences” & “high-school-biology” subsets).
  2. Open weights, open license. Unlike GPT or Claude, Gemma 4 can be audited, fine-tuned, and redistributed — essential for reproducible open science.
  3. Local, zero-cost inference. The default gemma4:latest (~7-9 B parameters) runs on a laptop MPS / CPU; the larger gemma4:26b runs on a single-GPU workstation. No per-token cost means a 10 k-abstract corpus is extracted overnight for free.
  4. Deterministic extraction with format="json". Ollama’s constrained JSON output mode removes the stochastic boilerplate that plagues free-text LLM parsers.

The extractor prompt

edaphos uses a single tight prompt, shared across all three backends for exact parity:

You are a causal-inference expert annotating pedology and soil-science
literature.

Your task: extract the explicit causal claims made by the passage
below. Return a JSON object with a single key "claims" whose value
is an array. Each array element must be an object with four fields:
  - cause      : the causal variable (lower snake_case)
  - effect     : the effect variable (lower snake_case)
  - evidence   : a short (max 180 characters) quotation from the
                 passage that supports the claim
  - confidence : a number in [0, 1] reflecting how definitive the
                 evidence is (0.9 = unambiguous causal phrasing,
                 0.5 = suggestive, 0.2 = speculative)

Only extract claims that are EXPLICITLY SUPPORTED by the passage.
Do not invent relationships. Return an empty array if none are
present. Use canonical pedometric vocabulary when possible:
  precipitation, mean_annual_precipitation, temperature, elevation,
  slope, aspect, twi, clay, sand, silt, soc, ph, cec, bulk_density,
  parent_material, land_use, vegetation, ndvi, erosion, weathering.

Output JSON object only, no prose, no markdown fences.

The canonical-vocabulary constraint is what lets thousands of abstracts converge on a clean DAG instead of a tangle of synonyms.

Single-abstract ingestion 

kg <- causal_kg_new()

kg <- causal_llm_ingest_abstract(
  kg,
  abstract = "In Cerrado Oxisols, higher mean annual precipitation
              drives organic-matter accumulation; steeper slopes
              enhance erosional SOC loss; long-standing native
              vegetation elevates topsoil nitrogen relative to
              converted pasture.",
  source   = "Ferreira 2021",
  backend  = "ollama",
  model    = "gemma4:latest"
)

causal_augment_diff(causal_cerrado_dag(),
                    causal_augment_dag(causal_cerrado_dag(), kg,
                                       min_confidence = 0.7))
#>                           cause              effect origin
#> 1                          elev              map_mm   base
#> 2                          elev               slope   base
#> ...
#> 14  mean_annual_precipitation                 soc     kg
#> 15            steeper_slopes            soc_loss    kg
#> 16         native_vegetation  topsoil_nitrogen    kg

Ten curated Cerrado-pedology abstracts and their Gemma-4 extractions ship in inst/extdata/cerrado_abstracts.jsonl + inst/extdata/cerrado_claims.jsonl, so the vignette builds fully offline on CI.

📈 Scaling from 10 to 10 000 abstracts

Three additions promote the extractor from demo to literature-scale:

  • Paginated corpus clients. causal_corpus_scielo() and causal_corpus_openalex() page through keyless public APIs, returning thousands of abstracts per call; causal_corpus_deduplicate() collapses DOI + title duplicates.
  • Resumable cached ingestion. causal_llm_ingest_corpus() takes cache_dir and max_retries. Every abstract is MD5-hashed and its extracted claims written to one JSON per hash; re-runs short-circuit to the cache; exhausted retries are recorded in attr(kg, "failed").
  • Live AGROVOC SPARQL alignment. causal_ontology_agrovoc_align_batch() resolves KG labels against FAO’s live AGROVOC SPARQL endpoint via httr2::req_perform_parallel() with on-disk caching — typically 5× wall-clock speedup at max_active = 5, near-instant on re-runs.

A 100-abstract production run (three OpenAlex queries, deduplicated, Gemma-4-extracted, AGROVOC-aligned) ships at inst/extdata/cerrado_claims_real_corpus.jsonl and is reproduced end-to-end by data-raw/run_large_corpus.R.

🗳️ Multi-extractor LLM voting

A single LLM backend inherits that model’s idiosyncrasies: GPT tends to over-generate claims, Claude to under-specify confidence, Gemma to be the strictest. causal_llm_vote() runs all three on the same abstract and resolves disagreements by one of three rules:

cons <- causal_llm_vote(
  abstract = "Higher MAP drives SOC in Cerrado...",
  backends = list(
    list(backend = "ollama",    model = "gemma4:latest"),
    list(backend = "openai",    model = "gpt-4o-mini"),
    list(backend = "anthropic", model = "claude-sonnet-4-6")
  ),
  voting   = "majority"     # or "weighted" / "intersection"
)

The formal resolution rule for majority voting is

claim(c→e)∈Ccons⇔|{b∈B:(c→e)∈Cb}|≥⌈|B|/2⌉, \text{claim}\,(c \to e) \in C_{\text{cons}} \;\iff\; \bigl|\{b \in B \,:\, (c \to e) \in C_b\}\bigr| \;\ge\; \lceil |B|/2 \rceil,

with confidence set to the per-backend mean over the voters that agreed. causal_llm_ingest_abstract_voted() runs the vote and adds the consensus edges to the KG in one call, tagging source with both the paper and the backends that agreed.

📂 Persistence, Turtle export and audit

Pillar 1 is not just an in-memory toy:

  • causal_kg_save() / causal_kg_load() — serialise through the tidy edge list (not through igraph’s raw C layout), guaranteeing portability across igraph versions and byte-reproducibility.
  • causal_kg_to_turtle() — emits a W3C-conformant RDF 1.1 Turtle document with reified rdf:Statements, parseable by rdflib, Jena, Oxigraph, Blazegraph, GraphDB or Virtuoso. Pure R, zero RDF dependencies.
  • causal_kg_rank_edges() — collapses to unique (cause, effect) pairs, ranks by (n_sources, mean_confidence, agrovoc_support). Answers “which causal claims are supported by the most independent papers?” in one call.
  • causal_structure_learn() (v1.1.0) — bottom-up DAG learning from data via four bnlearn algorithms (hc, tabu, pc-stable, mmhc) with whitelist / blacklist of pedological priors + bootstrap edge strengths.

Real-data results: 3 077 Cerrado profiles

We estimate backdoor-adjusted associations — not identified causal effects — on 3 077 real WoSIS topsoil profiles over the Cerrado, with covariates drawn from WorldClim 2.1, SoilGrids and Copernicus tree cover (all fetched from public endpoints; see data-raw/causal_cerrado_real_rebuild.R). Following Zhang & Wadoux (2026), we do not claim causal sufficiency; instead each effect carries a Cinelli–Hazlett robustness value (RV): the share of residual variance an unobserved confounder would need to explain in both exposure and outcome to drive the estimate to zero. Confidence intervals are a block bootstrap (B = 500) over 20 k-means spatial clusters. Every figure below is reproduced from the shipped causal_cerrado_real_v2.rds and pinned by test-causal-real-bundle.R.

Exposure Naive β Adjusted β 95% CI Significant? RV
MAP (g/kg per mm) 0.0082 0.0097 [0.0028, 0.0186] yes 0.16
MAT (g/kg per °C) −0.467 −0.824 [−1.37, 0.22] no 0.08
Tree cover (g/kg per 0–1) 2.86 0.35 [−3.31, 2.94] no 0.01
Clay (g/kg per %) 0.446 0.449 [0.29, 0.64] yes 0.18

Two effects survive as robust, mechanistically coherent associations: precipitation and clay content both raise topsoil carbon, and each would need a confounder explaining ~16–18 % of residual variance to overturn. The temperature effect has the expected (decomposition) sign but is not distinguishable from zero. The tree-cover row is the confounding demonstration: its naive association (2.86) all but disappears once climate is adjusted for (0.35, CI spanning zero, RV 0.01) — the raw signal was mostly shared climatic ancestry, exactly the pattern Zhang & Wadoux (2026) warn is misread as causal. Each effect is returned as an edaphos_posterior, so uncertainty_calibrate() applies uniformly (see §9).

Causal-discovery trio: expert × LLM × data-driven

vignette("causal-discovery-trio") asks a harder question: do the three DAG-construction strategies in Pillar 1 agree? Running all five methods on the same 1 095 WoSIS profiles:

Comparison Structural Hamming Distance
Expert ↔︎ LLM-augmented 0
bnlearn hc ↔︎ bnlearn tabu 0
bnlearn pc-stable ↔︎ hc 12
Expert ↔︎ bnlearn hc 29

The LLM adds nothing here, and that is the informative result. Of the 30 claims in inst/extdata/cerrado_claims.jsonl, only 3 have both endpoints expressible among the 10 WoSIS covariates, and all 3 were already in the expert DAG. The 32 remaining distinct concepts — decomposition, primary_mineral_dissolution, argillic_horizon, root_input, effective_cation_exchange_capacity, twi and others — have no counterpart in the covariate set. The extractor is not the bottleneck; the covariate set is.

Earlier releases reported SHD(Expert, LLM-augmented) = 2 and read it as the LLM being “conservative”. That figure came from six edges typed by hand into data-raw/causal_discovery_benchmark.R, carrying confidences (0.90, 0.82, 0.78, 0.75, 0.72, 0.71) that appear in no file in this package — every shipped claim has confidence 0.9. Those edges have been withdrawn; the benchmark now derives its edge set from the claims file through an explicit concept → column mapping that is validated against the columns which actually exist.

The finding that survives is the disagreement between expert and data-driven structure. The backdoor adjustment set for MAP → SOC is 5 covariates under the expert DAG (slope, wc_bio_01, wc_landcover_cropland, wc_landcover_grassland, wc_landcover_trees) but 1 under pc-stable (wc_bio_01) and 2 under hc/tabu. That difference directly changes the identified effect, so the three strategies are complementary, not substitutable, and the vignette recommends reporting the sensitivity rather than picking one.

📖 Vignettes: vignette("pilar1-causal"), vignette("causal-discovery-trio"). The real-data Cerrado application ships as the bundled causal_cerrado_real.rds and is exercised from vignette("case-cerrado-end-to-end"); it has no vignette of its own.

Multi-backend LLM extraction: harness, not vendor comparison

Pillar 1’s extractor can be driven by three backends (local Ollama, OpenAI, Anthropic) through causal_llm_extract(), and causal_llm_vote() combines them. A gold standard of 30 Cerrado abstracts × 72 expert-annotated causal claims (inst/extdata/cerrado_gold_standard_v1.jsonl) is shipped so the scoring harness can be exercised offline.

No measured vendor comparison is published here. The shipped bundle inst/extdata/llm_benchmark_results.rds carries mode = "simulated": it is the output of llm_benchmark_simulate(), a deterministic noise model whose precision, recall, latency and cost are inputs supplied by the caller (see the sim_args list in data-raw/llm_benchmark_run.R). Earlier releases of this README presented those inputs as a measured head-to-head table of Gemma, GPT-4o-mini and Claude scores. No API was ever called to produce them, so the table has been withdrawn.

What the simulated bundle legitimately demonstrates is that the harness works end to end: scoring against the gold standard, pairwise agreement, cost and latency accounting, and the voting rules all run deterministically in CI without network access or API keys.

To produce a real comparison, set EDAPHOS_USE_REAL_LLM=1, provide the API keys, and re-run data-raw/llm_benchmark_run.R; the bundle it writes will carry mode = "real", and tests/testthat/test-headline-claims.R will then permit a vendor-attributed table in this section.

📖 Vignette: vignette("llm-annotation-workflow"). The benchmark itself ships as llm_benchmark_results.rds + cerrado_gold_standard_v1.jsonl; there is no separate vignette.

v1.8.1 — Annotation tool: pre-annotation + Shiny review UI

The v1.8.0 benchmark runs on a 72-claim seed; a publication-grade paper needs ~300 claims with statistical power. v1.8.1 ships the two-phase annotation tooling to get there in ~3 hours:

# 1. LLM drafts one set of claims per abstract (~25 min for 100 abs.)
edaphos::llm_preannotate(
  corpus      = "cerrado_corpus_openalex.jsonl",
  backend     = "ollama",       # or "simulator" if Ollama absent
  model       = "gemma4:latest",
  output_path = "draft_gold_v2.jsonl",
  cache_dir   = "~/.cache/edaphos_annotation"
)

# 2. Shiny reviewer — pedologist accepts / edits / rejects / adds
edaphos::llm_annotation_launch(
  draft_path  = "draft_gold_v2.jsonl",
  output_path = "reviewed_gold_v2.jsonl",
  keyboard_shortcuts = TRUE
)

# 3. Export: drops rejected / untouched drafts + validates schema
edaphos::llm_annotation_export(
  reviewed_path = "reviewed_gold_v2.jsonl",
  output_path   = "cerrado_gold_standard_v2_final.jsonl"
)

The Shiny app has keyboard shortcuts (n = next, a = accept all, 1..9 = toggle per-claim accept) so a trained annotator processes ~2 abstracts/minute on simple cases. Every action writes to disk; interrupted sessions resume exactly where they left off.

📖 Vignette: vignette("llm-annotation-workflow").

v1.8.2 — App polish, OpenAlex corpus fetcher, Zenodo bundler

Four quality-of-life upgrades on top of the v1.8.1 skeleton:

  1. Real-corpus fetcher — data-raw/cerrado_corpus_v2_fetch.R hits 6 orthogonal OpenAlex queries on Cerrado pedogenesis, deduplicates (DOI + title), applies length and year filters, and writes a JSONL corpus of up to 150 real abstracts in the schema that llm_preannotate() consumes. EDAPHOS_CORPUS_MAILTO env-var lands you in OpenAlex’s polite pool (~10 req/s) for free.

  2. DAG preview tab — the Shiny reviewer now has a live DiagrammeR-rendered DAG of all accepted claims, with a min_support slider, edge colour by polarity (green/red), edge width by mean confidence, and an optional labels toggle. You see the KG emerging as you annotate.

  3. Dark mode — a bslib theme toggle in the sidebar (uses the native input_dark_mode() control, switches between Flatly and Darkly bootswatch themes). Respects your OS preference and repaints the whole UI on change, including the claim-row status colours.

  4. Zenodo packager — new tab “Publish” + exported function llm_annotation_to_zenodo() that builds a deposit-ready bundle:

    zenodo_package/
  ├── gold_standard.jsonl    (cleaned JSONL)
  ├── kg.ttl                 (RDF 1.1 Turtle)
  ├── metadata.json          (DataCite-compatible)
  └── README.md              (provenance + citation)
zenodo_package.zip           (upload-ready archive)

    Upload to zenodo.org/deposit/new and mint your own DOI for the KG as a standalone research artefact.

v1.9.0 — Foundation embeddings as causal instrumental variables

The Pillar 1 × Pillar 4 bridge. Backdoor adjustment (Pillar 1) identifies causal effects only under causal sufficiency — all confounders observed. When unobserved confounders U remain, the adjusted estimator is biased:

β̂backdoor=βtrue+bias(U)\hat{\beta}_{\text{backdoor}} = \beta_{\text{true}} + \text{bias}(U)

Instrumental variables (IVs) identify effects under a different set of assumptions [@Wooldridge2010]:

  1. Relevance: Cov(Z,X)≠0\text{Cov}(Z, X) \neq 0
  2. Exclusion: Z→YZ \to Y only through XX
  3. Unconfoundedness: Z⟂UZ \perp U

The MoCo v2 encoder (Pillar 4), trained contrastively on landscape patches without ever seeing SOC, is a natural IV candidate: it captures landscape-scale structure orthogonal to the named confounders in the DAG.

# 2SLS with foundation-model embeddings as instruments
iv_fit <- edaphos::causal_iv_from_embeddings(
  data       = cerrado_profiles,
  embeddings = foundation_embeddings,    # (n x 128) MoCo v2 output
  exposure   = "map",
  outcome    = "soc",
  covariates = c("mat","slope","elev","clay","sand","bd","trees"),
  n_pcs      = 5L   # top-5 PCs as instruments
)
iv_fit
#> <edaphos_causal_iv>
#>   map -> soc  (estimator: 2SLS, n = 3020)
#>   instruments : PC_1, PC_2, PC_3, PC_4, PC_5
#>   effect      : 0.0039  (OLS 0.0063; backdoor OLS 0.0075)
#>   stage-1 F   : 4630   (instruments very relevant)
#>   Sargan J    : p = 2.0e-17   (over-identification rejected)

Synthetic DGP validation (known truth β = 1.5):

Estimator β̂ 95% CI
OLS (biased by U) 1.82 [1.77, 1.87]
2SLS (IV) 1.46 [1.39, 1.53]
True 1.50 —

The synthetic check confirms the estimator recovers a known truth when its assumptions hold. The real-data result is a negative one, and that is the point. The MoCo v2 encoder here is real — 7 channels, 12 000 tiles, 3 000 epochs on-device (Metal), InfoNCE 7.2 → 5.2 — not a proxy. Its embedding PCs are extremely relevant instruments (stage-1 F ≈ 1 955, covariate-adjusted 2SLS), yet they decisively fail the Sargan over-identification test (p ≈ 3 × 10⁻¹³). A learned landscape representation does not manufacture a valid instrument: it encodes climate, terrain, soil and vegetation together, so it reaches SOC through many paths and violates the exclusion restriction. This is the empirical face of Zhang & Wadoux (2026)’s argument that causal sufficiency — and, here, instrument validity — is seldom achievable in DSM from observational data. IV does not rescue identification; the honest report is the failed test, not a headline effect.

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar1-pilar4-iv").

Foundation-model embeddings as instruments: what the Sargan test actually says

Two functions close the loop from the identification argument to empirical evidence:

  • foundation_embed_at_coords(moco, coords, stack, dataset, ...) extracts one embedding per query coordinate by cutting a patch_size x patch_size window, normalising, and running the encoder forward — 17 s for 1 095 WoSIS profiles on Apple M1 Max MPS.
  • foundation_build_cerrado_stack(bbox, ...) assembles the 31-channel SoilGrids + WorldClim + SRTM stack the encoder was trained on (measured: 1.84 GB downloaded, 3.0 min, cached to disk).

Using the Zenodo-published edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1 encoder on the 1 095 Cerrado profiles, at the encoder’s native 0.01-deg grid:

Exposure Stage-1 F Sargan p Over-identification
MAP → SOC 862 0.250 not rejected
Tree cover → SOC 8.4 0.042 rejected
Clay → SOC 11.0 0.0030 rejected

The result is partial, and that is the finding. For mean annual precipitation the instruments are strong (F = 862) and the over-identification restriction is not rejected: an encoder pretrained by contrastive self-supervision without ever seeing SOC does yield structurally valid instruments for that exposure, and the 2SLS estimate (β = 0.0126) is 64 % larger than the backdoor-OLS estimate (β = 0.0077), the direction expected when attenuation from covariate measurement error is corrected.

For tree cover and clay the same instruments fail. Tree cover also has a first-stage F of 8.4, below the conventional threshold of 10, so its 2SLS estimate should not be read as identified at all. Clay’s Sargan p = 0.003 rejects exclusion outright.

Three limitations that bound every number above.

  1. The encoder’s training normalisation was never persisted. The weights registry has no per-channel mean/sd for edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1, so the exact standardisation it was trained under is unrecoverable. The figures above use per-channel statistics computed over this area of interest, which is an approximation, not a reconstruction. The bundle records this as normalisation_source = "aoi". Every future encoder must publish its statistics; the registry now carries a norm_stats_status field so the gap is visible rather than assumed away.
  2. The area of interest exceeds the training region. The WoSIS profiles span 18.4° × 21.9°; the encoder was trained on the Cerrado core, 10° × 13°. The bundle records aoi_exceeds_training = TRUE. 21.8 % of the encoder’s 64 backbone channels are dead (exactly zero after post-ReLU average pooling) on this input, against roughly 5 % for input drawn from the distribution it was trained on.
  3. These are single-run values. Sargan p = 0.042 for tree cover sits close enough to 0.05 that it should not be treated as a sharp verdict without a resampling study.

Earlier releases of this README reported Sargan p of 0.343 / 0.283 / 0.424 for the three exposures and concluded that the test passed for all of them. Those figures were produced with the normalisation placeholder means = 0, sds = 1, which fed raw geophysical magnitudes into a network trained on standardised inputs and killed about half its channels. They have been withdrawn and replaced by the table above. tests/testthat/test-headline-claims.R now asserts every figure in this section against the shipped inst/extdata/causal_iv_cerrado_real.rds, so the two cannot drift apart again.

v1.9.2 — Cinelli & Hazlett (2020) sensitivity analysis

The Sargan test validates instrument exclusion; sensitivity analysis quantifies robustness to residual confounding after the fact. Following [@CinelliHazlett2020] we compute the Robustness Value (RV): the minimum partial R² that an unobserved confounder would need to have with both X and Y to zero out the estimate.

# Any of the following produces a RV summary
s <- edaphos::causal_sensitivity_summary(effect = 0.00769,
                                           se     = 0.00271,
                                           df     = 1084)
s$rv         # -> 0.083   (8.3% of residual variance)
s$rv_alpha   # -> 0.026   (threshold for significance loss)

# Or wrap an `lm` / `edaphos_causal_iv`:
edaphos::causal_sensitivity_from_lm(fit, exposure = "map")
edaphos::causal_sensitivity_from_iv(iv_fit)

Robustness table on the 1 095 Cerrado profiles:

Exposure Estimator β̂ RV RV @ 5%
MAP (mm/a) Naive OLS 0.0072 9.2% 3.7%
MAP (mm/a) Backdoor OLS 0.0077 8.3% 2.6%
MAP (mm/a) Proxy IV (v1.9.0) 0.0081 8.6% 3.0%
MAP (mm/a) Real MoCo IV (v1.9.1) 0.0169 3.9% 0.0%
Tree cover Backdoor OLS 6.54 6.3% 0.5%
Tree cover Real MoCo IV 4.98 0.9% 0.0%
Clay (%) Naive OLS 0.526 24.4% 19.8%
Clay (%) Backdoor OLS 0.192 5.0% 0.0%
Clay (%) Real MoCo IV 0.858 3.9% 0.0%

Scientific finding. The only robust causal claim in the Cerrado stack is Clay → SOC under Naive OLS (RV = 24%): no plausible confounder explaining less than a quarter of the residual variance could zero it out. MAP → SOC under Backdoor OLS is moderately robust (RV ≈ 8%); under real-encoder IV it drops to ≈ 4%, because the synthetic-stack mode yields weak instruments (Stage-1 F ≈ 10) and an inflated SE. A real-covariate run should lift F and reduce the SE, restoring RV — but note that the EDAPHOS_IV_REAL_STACK switch this README once told readers to set is read nowhere in the package. The real-stack path is a roadmap item, not a flag.

The package was validated against the published Cinelli-Hazlett Theorem 4.4 example to four decimal places (RV = 0.1810 expected, 0.1810 computed).

Pillar 2 — Physics-Informed ML

Motivation

Classical depth-harmonisation uses equal-area splines [Bishop et al. 1999] — a purely mathematical object disconnected from pedogenesis. Pillar 2 replaces the spline with a physics-informed kinetic of clay illuviation / organic-matter decay, parameterised either analytically or by a neural network and integrated end-to-end.

Alignment with Zhang & Wadoux (2026). The pedogenetic ODE is the closest this package comes to their generative causality: the soil property arises from a process the modeller writes down, which is their condition 1 (an explicit model). It does not satisfy their condition 3, faithfulness — that is a property of the data relative to a graph, not of an equation, and the DAG this package ships fails its own implied-independence test (see causal_dag_test()). Earlier versions of this README claimed both conditions; the claim about faithfulness was a category error.

Note also that the equation in this section is not itself derived from a process: it is the Russell & Moore (1968) exponential depth function with a fourth shape parameter. piml_profile_fit_mechanistic() is the derived alternative, from the steady-state advection-reaction balance, and on real multi-horizon profiles it is also the more accurate of the two.

Governing object

Depth-dependent translocation toward an equilibrium coordinate y∞y_\infty — which, because the rate decays with depth, is not the value the profile reaches (see the note below the equation),

dydz=−λ0e−μz(y(z)−y∞)(parametric)ordydz=fθ(z,y,𝐱)(Neural ODE). \frac{dy}{dz} \;=\; -\,\lambda_0\,e^{-\mu z}\,\bigl(y(z) - y_\infty\bigr) \qquad\text{(parametric)} \qquad\text{or}\qquad \frac{dy}{dz} \;=\; f_\theta\bigl(z, y, \mathbf{x}\bigr) \qquad\text{(Neural ODE).}

The parametric form is separable, so it is solved in closed form rather than integrated numerically, and fitted through a horizon-average observation operator; the Neural ODE form uses a fixed-step Runge-Kutta integrator in torch so training back-propagates through the whole trajectory [Chen et al. 2018].

Point and Bayesian APIs 

data(sp4, package = "aqp")
sp4$depth <- (sp4$top + sp4$bottom) / 2
colusa <- subset(sp4, id == "colusa")

# Point estimate
param  <- piml_profile_fit(colusa$depth, colusa$clay)

# Bayesian posterior. Laplace is the fast default; MCMC is what the paper
# reports, because on a real pedon Laplace narrows 5 of 7 intervals -- the
# observation noise by 1.8x -- being Gaussian on the log coordinates.
fit    <- piml_profile_fit_bayesian(colusa$depth, colusa$clay,
                                     method = "mcmc", seed = 1L)

# Neural ODE
neural <- piml_neural_ode_fit(
  colusa$depth, colusa$clay,
  hidden = c(16L, 16L), epochs = 500L, seed = 1L
)

# Deep ensemble (K = 5) — canonical uncertainty for the Neural ODE
ens <- piml_neural_ode_fit_ensemble(colusa$depth, colusa$clay, K = 5L)

predict(fit, newdepths = c(10, 20, 40, 80),
        interval = 0.95, include_obs_noise = TRUE, seed = 1L)

The fitted parameters carry pedological meaning — y0 ≈ 19 % is the clay extrapolated to the surface, mu says whether translocation accelerates or slows with depth — but this pedon also shows the limit of that reading. Its four horizons stop at 42 cm and the clay is still rising, so the model has no information about where the argillic horizon levels off, and print() says so:

  NOTE: the deepest horizon (36 cm) has travelled only 0% of the
        way to y(Inf), so the deep value is an extrapolation, not an
        estimate. Do not read it as a parent-material value.

Earlier versions of this README quoted y_inf ≈ 62 % here and called it the argillic asymptote. That number was not estimated from the data: the L2 penalty was applied to the raw y_inf, so it scaled with the square of the property’s units and pinned the value. Removing the penalty on the same four horizons gives 533 %. The regulariser is now a scale-free shrinkage toward the observed range, and an unidentified asymptote is reported as unidentified. To estimate a parent-material value you need horizons deep enough to see the profile flatten.

The Neural ODE fits the same four horizons to tighter RMSE and is the default for non-monotonic profiles (E-below-A, buried paleosols).

Closing the Pillar 2 × Pillar 5 loop

al_physics_gate_piml() takes any PIML fit and turns it into a rejection gate that the Pillar 5 Active Learning loop uses to discard candidates whose predicted profile violates monotonicity, non-negativity, or plausible-range constraints. This is the concrete implementation of the “process-informed filter” that Zhang & Wadoux (2026) advocate: model candidates aren’t just ranked by statistical uncertainty but also by physical plausibility.

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar2-piml-profile").

Pillar 3 — 4D Pedometry

Motivation

Most digital soil maps report a time-invariant field, which is ecologically false: topsoil SOC responds measurably to climate forcing on monthly-to-annual scales [Lehmann and Kleber 2015; Minasny et al. 2017]. Zhang and Wadoux (2026) explicitly flag this as a weakness of successionist DSM: “soil measurements and observations capture only a snapshot emerging from a complex, dynamic system, without clear temporal sequencing.”

Pillar 3 adds the time dimension with a stacked Convolutional LSTM [Shi et al. 2015] and a stochastic Ensemble Kalman Filter [Evensen 1994] for assimilating new in-situ observations.

Governing object

A multi-layer ConvLSTM propagates a spatial hidden state 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_t and cell state 𝐂t\mathbf{C}_t alongside time:

𝐢t=σ(Wxi*𝐗t+Whi*𝐇t−1),𝐟t=σ(Wxf*𝐗t+Whf*𝐇t−1),𝐠t=tanh⁡(Wxg*𝐗t+Whg*𝐇t−1),𝐨t=σ(Wxo*𝐗t+Who*𝐇t−1),𝐂t=𝐟t⊙𝐂t−1+𝐢t⊙𝐠t,𝐇t=𝐨t⊙tanh⁡(𝐂t), \begin{aligned} \mathbf{i}_t &= \sigma\bigl(W_{xi} * \mathbf{X}_t + W_{hi} * \mathbf{H}_{t-1}\bigr), \\ \mathbf{f}_t &= \sigma\bigl(W_{xf} * \mathbf{X}_t + W_{hf} * \mathbf{H}_{t-1}\bigr), \\ \mathbf{g}_t &= \tanh\bigl(W_{xg} * \mathbf{X}_t + W_{hg} * \mathbf{H}_{t-1}\bigr), \\ \mathbf{o}_t &= \sigma\bigl(W_{xo} * \mathbf{X}_t + W_{ho} * \mathbf{H}_{t-1}\bigr), \\ \mathbf{C}_t &= \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \mathbf{g}_t, \\ \mathbf{H}_t &= \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\mathbf{C}_t), \end{aligned}

with * a 2-D convolution and ⊙ the Hadamard product.

Example 

cube   <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 12L, W = 12L, T_total = 18L, seed = 7L)
past   <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube, t_slice = 1:12)
future <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube, t_slice = 13:18)

fit <- temporal_convlstm_fit(
  past$sequence, past$target,
  hidden_dims     = c(12L, 6L),        # stacked ConvLSTM
  kernel_size     = 3L,
  return_sequence = TRUE,
  epochs          = 120L, lr = 0.02,
  seed            = 1L
)
forecast <- temporal_convlstm_rollout(
  fit,
  past_sequence  = past$sequence,
  future_drivers = future$sequence
)

🎯 Stochastic EnKF with Gaspari-Cohn localization (v1.5.0)

In a realistic DSM pipeline, new in-situ observations keep arriving after the ConvLSTM was trained. temporal_kalman_update() nudges the trained forecast toward those new observations with a stochastic Ensemble Kalman Filter [Evensen 1994; Burgers, van Leeuwen and Evensen 1998]: a gain matrix is estimated directly from the ensemble sample covariance and applied per-member, so the posterior ensemble reflects the new evidence without retraining.

The default localization is Gaspari-Cohn — a compactly supported 5th-order polynomial that tapers the gain smoothly to zero at twice the specified radius, preventing spurious long-range correlations typical of small ensembles.

fc_ens <- array(..., dim = c(K = 10, H = 10, W = 10))

assim <- temporal_kalman_update(
  forecast_ensemble   = fc_ens,
  obs_value           = c(0.62, 0.58, 0.51),
  obs_row             = c(5L, 10L, 15L),
  obs_col             = c(5L, 10L, 15L),
  obs_sd              = 0.02,
  localization_radius = 2                    # Gaspari-Cohn taper
)

Real-data demonstration (v1.5.0)

The bundled temporal_cerrado_results.rds holds the full pipeline run on a real Cerrado 2° × 2° AoI cube (MOD13Q1 NDVI + NASA POWER precipitation + NASA POWER T2M, 168 monthly steps, 2003 – 2016), with:

  • 10 × 10 grid at 0.2° resolution
  • K = 10-member ConvLSTM ensemble
  • 8 synthetic in-situ observations for the EnKF test
  • localization radius = 2 cells
Metric Prior (ConvLSTM) Analysis (EnKF + localization) Reduction
RMSE (COS, normalised) 0.637 0.617 −3.2%

The Kalman gain map becomes the first priority signal for the Pillar 5 active-learning loop — cells with large gain would benefit most from another in-situ sample.

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar3-4d-soc"). The real-AoI run above is distributed as a result bundle rather than as a vignette.

Pillar 4 — Foundation Models

Motivation

Labelled soil samples are expensive; covariate rasters are abundant. Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) [Chen et al. 2020; Jean et al. 2019] pre-trains an encoder on unlabelled raster patches and reuses the resulting representation as a learned feature map — the premise of a future “SoilGPT”.

Governing object

For each batch of BB raster patches, SimCLR draws two stochastic augmentations per patch, encodes each with a shared backbone CNN and projection head, and minimises the normalised temperature-scaled cross-entropy loss [Chen et al. 2020]:

ℒNT-Xent=−12B∑i=1B∑v∈{1,2}log⁡exp⁡(sim(𝐳i(v),𝐳i(v′))/τ)∑k≠(i,v)exp⁡(sim(𝐳i(v),𝐳k)/τ). \mathcal{L}_{\text{NT-Xent}} \;=\; -\frac{1}{2B} \sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{v\in\{1,2\}} \log \frac{\exp\!\bigl(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{z}^{(v)}_{i},\,\mathbf{z}^{(v')}_{i}) / \tau\bigr)} {\displaystyle\sum_{k \neq (i,v)} \exp\!\bigl(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{z}^{(v)}_{i},\,\mathbf{z}_{k})/\tau\bigr)}.

After pre-training the projection head is discarded and the backbone output fθ(𝐱)f_\theta(\mathbf{x}) is reused as the downstream feature vector. MoCo v2 [He et al. 2020; Chen et al. 2020b] replaces the two-view symmetric loss with a queue-based momentum encoder, scaling to larger batches.

Zenodo-hosted pre-trained weights 

moco <- foundation_weights_load("edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1", verbose = TRUE)
fit  <- foundation_fit_classifier(
  moco, labelled_patches, soil_order,
  freeze_backbone = TRUE, head = "linear",
  epochs = 40L, device = "mps", seed = 1L
)
predict(fit, new_patches, type = "prob")

The first published encoder — edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1 — was pre-trained on Apple M1 Max (MPS) over 50 000 16 × 16 tiles of a core Cerrado AoI (longitude −53 to −43, latitude −23 to −10), stacking SoilGrids 250 m, WorldClim 2.1 and SRTM 30-arc-second. Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19701276. An encoder v2 (200 k steps, 10× the v1 budget) is currently in training; v1.3.2 will re-benchmark with the new weights.

🔀 Deep-ensemble + MC-dropout (v1.6.0)

Pillar 4 was deterministic through v1.5.0. v1.6.0 ships two canonical uncertainty recipes:

  • foundation_finetune_ensemble(K = 5L) — K independent heads on the same encoder, different seeds [Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017].
  • foundation_mcdropout_predict() — N Monte-Carlo dropout forward passes with the dropout layers left active at predict time [Gal and Ghahramani 2016].

Both wrap into an edaphos_posterior, so uncertainty_calibrate() applies identically.

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar4-simclr-embeddings").

Pillar 5 — Autonomous Active Learning

Motivation

Traditional DSM decouples sampling design from model fitting — a pre-defined scheme collects observations, then a model is trained on whatever landed. This discards the fact that, once an initial model exists, its uncertainty field is direct guidance on where additional information is most needed [Settles 2009; Brus 2019]. Pillar 5 closes the loop: fit → query → measure → refit.

Governing object

A hybrid batch-mode acquisition policy,

πhyb(𝐱;α)=αũt(𝐱)+(1−α)d̃t(𝐱),α∈[0,1], \pi_{\text{hyb}}(\mathbf{x};\alpha) \;=\;\alpha\,\tilde{u}_t(\mathbf{x}) \;+\; (1-\alpha)\,\tilde{d}_t(\mathbf{x}), \qquad \alpha\in[0,1],

where ũt\tilde{u}_t is the Quantile Regression Forest [Meinshausen 2006] prediction-interval width and d̃t\tilde{d}_t is the min-distance feature-space diversity from the already-labelled set. A "cost" variant adds a logistical-distance penalty for autonomous sampler deployment; a physics_gate keyword rejects physically implausible candidates via a PIML fit (the Pillar 2 × 5 bridge).

Example 

covs <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi")

set.seed(42)
seed_idx <- al_initial_design(br_cerrado, covariates = covs, n = 25L, iter = 1500L)

set.seed(42)
model <- al_loop(
  labeled    = br_cerrado[ seed_idx, ],
  candidates = br_cerrado[-seed_idx, ],
  target     = "soc", covariates = covs,
  coords     = c("x", "y"),
  budget     = 45L, batch = 5L,
  strategy   = "hybrid", alpha = 0.7,
  num.trees  = 500L, verbose = FALSE
)
tail(al_history(model), 5)
#>    iter n_labeled rmse_oob mean_uncertainty
#> 6     5        50 5.387328          20.1760
#> 7     6        55 5.376662          19.1320
#> 8     7        60 5.294309          19.1900
#> 9     8        65 4.913287          18.3640
#> 10    9        70 4.942248          16.9916

OOB RMSE falls from 5.37 to 4.94 g/kg after nine batches of 5 samples. Queried points concentrate in transition zones between covariate regimes — exactly where expert pedologists historically placed transects.

🎲 BatchBALD (v1.1.0)

An information-theoretic alternative to the hybrid heuristic: al_query_batchbald() picks the batch that maximises the mutual information between its labels and the model parameters [Kirsch et al. 2019]:

BatchBALD(B)=I(yB;θ∣xB,𝒟). \mathrm{BatchBALD}(B) \;=\; I(y_B; \theta \mid x_B, \mathcal D).

For a QRF (the al_fit() backbone) the trees are the parameter samples, so the joint covariance of the epistemic posterior is the per-tree empirical covariance across candidates. Under Gaussian aleatoric noise σa2\sigma_a^2 the objective reduces to a log-determinant with a (1−1/e)(1 - 1/e) optimality guarantee [Nemhauser et al. 1978]. Incremental Cholesky / Schur-complement updates make every greedy step O(m2⋅npool)O(m^2 \cdot n_{\text{pool}}).

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar5-active-learning").

Pillar 6 — Quantum ML

Motivation

High-dimensional covariate stacks eventually hit the classical curse of dimensionality. Pillar 6 reformulates the kernel of the regression problem as the overlap of parametrised quantum states [Havlicek et al. 2019; Schuld and Killoran 2019], living in a Hilbert space of dimension 2n2^n in the number of qubits yet classically simulable in pure R for n≤8n \le 8.

What it does on this repository’s own benchmark. Fifth of six methods, RMSE 0.663 against 0.586 for ordinary least squares on DAG-selected covariates, and an NSE of −0.019 — that is, marginally worse than predicting the training-fold mean everywhere. The construction below is sound and the implementation is verified against a reference, but on this data set the quantum kernel does not buy accuracy, and the pillar is presented as a method that is available rather than one that is recommended. The four-way head-to-head later in this section reaches the same conclusion from a different angle.

Governing object

The ZZFeatureMap quantum state

|ϕ(𝐱)⟩=(Uϕ(𝐱)H⊗n)R|0⟩⊗n \lvert\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle \;=\; \bigl(U_\phi(\mathbf{x})\,H^{\otimes n}\bigr)^{R}\,\lvert 0\rangle^{\otimes n}

induces the kernel

K(𝐱i,𝐱j)=|⟨ϕ(𝐱j)∣ϕ(𝐱i)⟩|2, K(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) \;=\; \bigl\lvert \langle \phi(\mathbf{x}_j) \mid \phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\rangle \bigr\rvert^{2},

with

Uϕ(𝐱)=exp⁡(i∑S⊆[n]ϕS(𝐱)∏i∈SZi),ϕ{i}(𝐱)=2xi,ϕ{i,j}(𝐱)=2(π−xi)(π−xj). U_\phi(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; \exp\!\Bigl(i\!\sum_{S\subseteq[n]} \phi_S(\mathbf{x})\!\prod_{i\in S}\! Z_i\Bigr), \quad \phi_{\{i\}}(\mathbf{x}) = 2\,x_i, \quad \phi_{\{i,j\}}(\mathbf{x}) = 2\,(\pi - x_i)(\pi - x_j).

GP-equivalent posterior (v1.6.0)

Using the well-known equivalence between Kernel Ridge Regression and Gaussian-process regression [Rasmussen & Williams 2006 §2.3], the Q-KRR’s predictive variance is analytic:

σϵ2(𝐱⋆)=k(𝐱⋆,𝐱⋆)⏟aleatoric−k(𝐱⋆,X)(K+λI)−1k(X,𝐱⋆)⏟epistemic+σn2 \sigma_\epsilon^2(\mathbf{x}_\star) = \underbrace{k(\mathbf{x}_\star, \mathbf{x}_\star)}_{\text{aleatoric}} - \underbrace{k(\mathbf{x}_\star, X)\,(K + \lambda I)^{-1}\,k(X, \mathbf{x}_\star)}_{\text{epistemic}} + \sigma_n^2

where σn2\sigma_n^2 is the leave-one-out residual variance. quantum_krr_posterior() wraps this into an edaphos_posterior with the epistemic / aleatoric decomposition carried through the object.

Qiskit VQE pipeline (v0.9.0)

Three interchangeable execution backends for variational quantum eigensolvers:

ham <- quantum_hamiltonian_h2()

# 1) Exact noiseless statevector
quantum_vqe_fit(ham, backend = "aer_statevector", seed = 1L)

# 2) Shot-based Aer simulation with SPSA
quantum_vqe_fit(ham, backend = "aer_shots",
                shots = 4096L, optimizer = "SPSA",
                max_iter = 80L, seed = 1L)

# 3) Real IBM Quantum hardware with M3 readout mitigation
Sys.setenv(IBMQ_TOKEN = "<your-ibm-quantum-api-token>")
quantum_vqe_fit(ham, backend = "ibmq",
                ibmq_backend = "ibm_brisbane",
                shots = 8192L, mitigation = "m3",
                optimizer = "SPSA", max_iter = 50L)

Three organo-mineral Hamiltonians come pre-built via qiskit-nature + PySCF:

Variant Pedological role Active space Qubits
"formic_acid" carboxylate — dominant humic functional group (2e, 2o) 2
"methanediol" ortho-diol — catechol-style Fe(III) chelator (2e, 2o) 2
"ferric_formate" monodentate Fe(III)–OOCH — minimum viable organo-mineral (4e, 4o) 4

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar6-quantum").

v2.0.0 — Quantum kernel over foundation-model embeddings

The Pilar 4 × Pilar 6 fusion. Foundation embeddings (64-dim MoCo v2 outputs) are compressed to n_pcs principal components rescaled to [−π,π][-\pi, \pi], then lifted into a 2n2^n-dimensional Hilbert space by the ZZFeatureMap. Four new exported functions:

# 1. Reduce foundation embeddings to top-n PCs in quantum range
red <- edaphos::qf_embed_reduce(embeddings, n_pcs = 6L)

# 2. Compare quantum, RBF, and linear Gram matrices
cmp <- edaphos::qf_kernel_compare(red$X_q, reps = 2L)
cmp$diagnostics   # Frobenius distance + effective rank

# 3. Fit Quantum-KRR directly on foundation embeddings
fit <- edaphos::qf_krr_fit(embeddings, y,
                            n_pcs = 6L, reps = 2L, lambda = 0.5)

# 4. 4-way head-to-head benchmark
bm <- edaphos::qf_krr_benchmark(embeddings, covariates, y,
                                  n_pcs = 6L, reps = 2L, lambda = 0.5)

This benchmark is a negative control. The raster stack the encoder sees is white noise — stats::rnorm() into every cell of every channel (data-raw/quantum_foundation_benchmark.R) — so the “foundation embeddings” describe a landscape that carries no signal, by construction. Three of the four methods below predict from features that cannot contain information about SOC. Read it as a check that the pipeline reports failure when there is nothing to find, not as a covariate benchmark. For the real-covariate answer see the six-method table below.

5-fold spatial CV on 1 081 Cerrado profiles (synthetic-stack mode). The Cerrado pool holds 1 095 profiles; 14 lose their embedding at the complete.cases() step after the encoder pass, so the CV runs on 1 081. This table said 1 095 until the bundle was re-read.

Method RMSE MAE R² (pooled) R² (fold mean)
Quantum KRR on raw covariates 15.5 9.2 −0.075 −0.350
ranger (raw covariates) 15.5 9.0 −0.075 −0.795
Quantum KRR on foundation PCs 15.6 9.3 −0.089 −0.295
RBF-KRR on foundation PCs 16.1 9.8 −0.159 −0.449

Finding: all four are worse than predicting the mean. Every pooled R² is negative, so no method here beats the zero-parameter null — and that includes the classical ranger baseline, which is the honest result on noise features. The four are close to one another (−0.075 to −0.159) and the differences between them are not worth interpreting.

What this table used to say, and why. Until this run it read 0.00 for the three kernel methods and 0.08 for ranger, under the conclusion that the four regressors were statistically indistinguishable and that the quantum lift matched but did not surpass ranger. Those zeros were not measured. qf_krr_benchmark() computed max(0, 1 - SS_res/SS_tot), so every negative R² — 17 of the 20 fold-by-method values — was floored to exactly zero, which converts “worse than the mean” into “explains none of the variance”. Two different findings, and the clamp published the flattering one. The clamp is gone (R/quantum_foundation.R delegates to edaphos_r2(), which is Nash–Sutcliffe and unclamped) and the bundle has been rebuilt from the same script and seed.

Two R² columns, because one of them is unstable. edaphos_r2() is Nash–Sutcliffe against each test fold’s own mean, so a fold whose profiles happen to be homogeneous has a small denominator and a wild R². Fold 2 of this partition has sd(SOC) = 5.9 g/kg against 11–21 in the other four; ranger scores −4.28 there, and that single fold drags its fold-mean to −0.80 and makes it look like the worst of the four. Pooled over folds — one ratio of summed squares rather than a mean of ratios — ranger is −0.075, mid-pack. The pooled column is the one to read; the fold mean is shown so the instability is visible instead of smoothed away.

Earlier versions of this section listed three “testable explanations” for the null result — a synthetic stack, an undertrained encoder, too few qubits — and left them standing as though they were reasons to expect a different answer later. They are not. Each is a reason the run was uninformative; none is evidence that a corrected run would favour the quantum kernel. Two of the three have since been run, and both answered against it.

Proposed test Status Result
1. Real covariate stack instead of synthetic Run Negative. The six-method benchmark (inst/extdata/benchmark_wosis_6pilar.rds) scores quantum KRR on the real SoilGrids / WorldClim / SRTM covariates over 1,095 WoSIS profiles and 5 spatially blocked folds with a 68 km buffer: RMSE 0.663 against 0.583 for DAG-restricted OLS, NSE −0.024 — below the achievable null of the training-fold mean — and PICP90 0.663 against a nominal 0.90. It is also the most expensive method by a factor of 337 (762 s against 2.3 s).
2. Encoder trained 10× longer (moco-v2, 200k steps) Run Negative, indirectly. Foundation embeddings do reach the benchmark, as P4, and rank fourth of six (RMSE 0.616, NSE 0.118) — below both plain OLS and a quantile forest on raw covariates. The embedding route does not carry information the covariates lack; see the instrumental-variable result, where those embeddings are extremely relevant and decisively invalid.
3. 8–10 qubits instead of 6 Not run Open. We do not claim it would fail; we claim nothing about it, which is the honest position for an experiment nobody has done.

The contribution is infrastructure. qf_* functions formalise the Pilar 4 × Pilar 6 fusion and ship a reproducible benchmark. That benchmark has now been run on real inputs and returned a negative result, which is reported here rather than deferred to a future version.

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar4-pilar6-quantum").

Pillar 7 — Bayesian Hierarchical Spatial

Motivation

A machine-learning soil map returns a number per pixel; it rarely returns an honest interval, because residual spatial structure is treated as noise rather than as a signal with a covariance. Pillar 7 puts the dependence inside the model as a Gaussian-process random effect and returns a posterior over every quantity of interest [Banerjee et al. 2014].

Governing object

y=Xβ+w+ε,w∼GP(0,σ2R(ϕ)),ε∼N(0,τ2I), y = X\beta + w + \varepsilon, \qquad w \sim GP\big(0,\ \sigma^2 R(\phi)\big), \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0,\ \tau^2 I),

with R(ϕ)ij=exp⁡(−ϕ‖si−sj‖)R(\phi)_{ij} = \exp(-\phi \lVert s_i - s_j \rVert). Note that ϕ\phi is a rate (units 1/distance), not a range; the practical correlation range is ≈3/ϕ\approx 3/\phi.

Conditional on ϕ\phi every update is conjugate, so bhs_fit() profiles ϕ\phi by maximum likelihood over phi_range and runs a Metropolis-free Gibbs sampler for everything else — the same concession INLA makes [Rue et al. 2009]. The Cholesky-heavy inner loop runs through an RcppArmadillo backend.

fit <- bhs_fit(train, soc ~ elev + slope + twi, coords = c("x", "y"),
               nmcmc = 1500L, burn = 500L, phi_range = c(0.05, 1000))

pred <- predict(fit, newdata = test)   # Bayesian kriging, per draw

bhs_fit() warns when the profile-MLE of ϕ\phi lands on an endpoint of phi_range: the bracket rather than the data then set the correlation rate, and the spatial variance fraction is not interpretable. Read that warning before reading anything else — the vignette shows a case where the fraction reads 0.97 with a tight posterior in a fit that has no resolvable spatial field at all.

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar7-bayesian-hierarchical").

Pillar 8 — Neural Operators

Motivation

A soil profile is not a stack of independent points; it is a function of depth. Pillar 8 learns the operator that produced it, rather than a pointwise regression evaluated at fixed depths.

Governing object

𝒢:u(z)↦y(z) \mathcal{G} : u(z) \longmapsto y(z)

Two architectures, both shipped:

Fourier Neural Operator [Li et al. 2021] — spectral convolution with the spectrum truncated to n_modes:

(𝒦v)(z)=ℱ−1(Rθ⋅ℱv)(z) (\mathcal{K}v)(z) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\big(R_\theta \cdot \mathcal{F}v\big)(z)

DeepONet [Lu et al. 2021] — branch/trunk factorisation, the constructive form of the Chen and Chen (1995) universal operator approximation theorem:

𝒢(u)(z)≈∑k=1pbk(u)tk(z) \mathcal{G}(u)(z) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{p} b_k(u)\, t_k(z) 

don <- no_deeponet_fit(depths, targets, covariates,
                       branch_hidden = 24L, trunk_hidden = 24L)

# The trunk accepts any depth, including ones never trained on:
predict(don, new_covariates, newdepths = c(7.5, 33, 61, 97, 133))

That last line is the point of the pillar. On the training grid a quantile regression forest is at least as accurate; asked for depths it never saw, it is not. The vignette measures both.

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar8-neural-operators").

Pillar 9 — Diffusion Models

Motivation

Every other pillar answers “what is the value here?”. None answers “what does a plausible soil landscape look like?” — a map assembled from per-pixel quantiles is smoother than any real landscape and corresponds to no coherent realisation. Pillar 9 samples whole maps.

Governing object

Forward process (fixed, no parameters), on the cosine schedule of [Nichol and Dhariwal 2021]:

q(xt∣x0)=N(α‾tx0,(1−α‾t)I) q(x_t \mid x_0) = N\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_t) I\big)

Only the denoiser ϵθ(xt,t)\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) is learned, by score matching [Ho et al. 2020]; dm_sample() then runs ancestral sampling from t=Tt = T down to 00 with x0x_0 clipping.

sch <- dm_cosine_schedule(T = 100L)
fit <- dm_fit(patch_stack, T = 100L, epochs = 250L)
gen <- dm_sample(fit, n_samples = 4L)

Honest status. The pure-R backend trains a readout over frozen random features (an ELM regime) and does not reproduce the spatial autocorrelation of the training patches — measured, and reported in the vignette rather than hidden behind plausible-looking thumbnails. Use backend = "torch", which trains every layer by autograd and does recover the structure.

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar9-diffusion-models").

Pillar 10 — Graph Neural Networks

Motivation

Kriging assumes you know the covariance function; a random forest assumes profiles are independent rows. Neither is right — profiles inform each other through a relation that should be learned.

Governing object

Graph attention [Veličković et al. 2018] over a k-NN co-location graph of profiles:

eij=LeakyReLU(𝐚⊤[Whi‖Whj]),αij=exp⁡(eij)∑k∈𝒩(i)exp⁡(eik) e_{ij} = \mathrm{LeakyReLU}\!\big(\mathbf{a}^\top[W h_i \Vert W h_j]\big), \qquad \alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \exp(e_{ik})}

The softmax is grouped per neighbourhood, and eije_{ij} depends on both endpoints’ features — so two pairs at identical separation can receive very different weights. That is what a fixed covariance function cannot express.

g <- gnn_build_graph(profiles, k = 8L, feature_cols = feat,
                     edges = "spatial", self_loops = TRUE)

ens <- gnn_fit_ensemble(g, targets = profiles$soc,
                        train_mask = train_mask, n_ensemble = 5L)

Attention is trained by analytic reverse-mode gradients through the grouped softmax — hand-derived, and checked against central finite differences across several architectures in test-pilar10-gat-grad.R. train_mask keeps every node in message passing while restricting the loss to training nodes, so no test label reaches the optimiser. gnn_fit_ensemble() averages seeds so the published comparison against a 500-tree QRF is ensemble-versus-ensemble rather than one model against a forest.

📖 Vignette: vignette("pilar10-graph-attention").

Unified uncertainty API (v1.6.0)

Through v1.5.0 each pillar quantified uncertainty in its own format. v1.6.0 introduces one class — edaphos_posterior — and one calibration routine — uncertainty_calibrate() — that work identically for every pillar.

flowchart LR

    end
    subgraph UNI["edaphos_posterior"]

    end
    subgraph DIAG["uncertainty_calibrate()"]

        PICP["PICP @ p"]
        MPIW["MPIW @ p"]

        RMSE["point RMSE"]
    end

    N1 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT
    N2 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT
    N3 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT
    N4 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT
    N5 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT

Three lines of code are now enough to calibrate any pillar:

post <- causal_effect_posterior(data, dag, exposure, outcome, B = 500L)
cal  <- uncertainty_calibrate(post, truth = observed_effects)
autoplot(post)                       # ggplot2 figure by query type

Native-query calibration (v1.7.1)

Evaluating each pillar in its natural domain — not forced into a shared map query — gives the scientifically honest table:

Pillar Native query n CRPS PICP (90%) MPIW (90%) RMSE
P1 Causal effect β (g/kg per mm) 40 0.004 0.775 0.020 0.007
P2 PIML depth profile y(z) 9 1.971 0.778 6.608 4.096
P3 4D future map NDVI(t★) 100 0.366 0.700 1.268 0.637
P4 Found. 5-fold spatial CV 250 7.621 0.268 8.353 12.41
P5 AL held-out map 71 6.375 0.930 37.816 12.86
P6 Q-KRR held-out regression 75 8.203 0.840 35.632 16.94

How to read this table. The 90% nominal PICP should be close to 0.90. P5 AL (0.93) and P6 Q-KRR (0.84) are the best-calibrated spatial-query pillars; P1 (0.78) and P3 (0.70) are acceptable in their own domains despite small n. Two rows flag real failure modes, both reported rather than papered over. P4’s 0.27 comes from naïve ensembles of ranger heads underestimating epistemic SD, because ranger already marginalises over trees. P2’s 0.78 is the residue of two corrections. The row used to read 0.71 with an RMSE of 0.83, measured by leaving one horizon out of a seven-point profile that had been typed in by hand; on a real nine-horizon WoSIS profile reaching 550 cm the same procedure gave 0.44. Two things were wrong with that number and both are fixed. The interval being scored excluded observation noise, so a mean-function interval was being asked to cover a measured value it structurally cannot — restoring it takes the coverage to 0.67. And the likelihood was Gaussian on g/kg, which puts predictive mass below zero and weights every horizon by the same absolute error; a lognormal takes it to 0.78 and removes the negative draws entirely. The pedogenetic ODE is still overconfident at a nominal 0.90, and that is now the honest residual rather than an artefact of how it was scored. See vignette("capstone-cerrado-campaign") §10 for the side-by-side comparison with the naïve unified-query table and its caveats.

📖 Vignette: vignette("uncertainty-unified").

Capstone vignette (v1.7.0)

vignette("capstone-cerrado-campaign") is the flagship of v1.7.0 — a ~900-line narrative that puts the pillars to work on a single decision: where should we place 8 new field samples in the Cerrado?

What it contains

  • 📊 12 figures (ODE profile posteriors, EnKF gain maps, foundation-model SD maps, AL selection map, quantum-kernel decomposition, final decision map).
  • 📋 6 tables (LLM-extracted claims, causal effects, ODE parameters, AL selection, calibration diagnostic, decision matrix).
  • 🔁 1 flowchart of the six-pillar pipeline.
  • 📐 Full LaTeX derivations of the pedogenetic ODE and the Gaspari-Cohn taper.
  • 📚 Citations tied back to Zhang & Wadoux (2026) at every pillar.

The decision matrix

For each of the 8 sites, the vignette reports:

column Pilar Meaning
score_p5 5 Hybrid AL score (uncertainty + diversity)
qkrr_ep 6 Q-KRR epistemic SD
enkf_gain 3 Kalman gain magnitude at the site
found_sd 4 Foundation ensemble SD
map_effect 1 Backdoor-adjusted MAP → COS direct effect
ode_pred 2 ODE-predicted topsoil SOC (sanity check)
final_score 1-6 Weighted mean (weights declared in the vignette)

The narrative then justifies each ranked site causally:

Site 1. High EnKF gain (P3) indicates that SOC dynamics are changing fast here; high foundation-model SD (P4) confirms that the representation space is under-sampled. The ODE (P2) shows that k1k_1 carries 2× above-average posterior variance in this cell — a new sample here directly reduces uncertainty about the decomposition process.

Benchmarks on real data

As of v1.3.1 every performance claim against the classical regression-tree state of the art is backed by a reproducible real-data benchmark. The canonical case study runs on 1 095 real Cerrado topsoil profiles pulled live from WoSIS 2019 (Batjes et al. 2020, CC-BY-4.0), evaluated by 5-fold spatial cross-validation (k-means on coordinates), with covariates from SoilGrids 250 m, WorldClim 2.1, SRTM 30-arcsec, and ESA WorldCover 2020.

Method n RMSE (g/kg) MAE (g/kg) R² PICP @ 95 Interval score
B1 ranger QRF — 56 covariates 1095 13.51 7.72 0.219 0.944 65.8
B2 ranger + gstat residual kriging 893* 14.01 7.93 0.205 0.945 79.9
E ranger + MoCo v1 embedding 923* 14.07 7.95 0.157 0.940 71.7

* Kriging drops test points whose variogram-range disk misses the training cloud; the foundation stack drops points within 16 pixels of the Cerrado raster edge.

Honest reading. R² ≈ 0.22 is in line with published regional Brazilian / Cerrado SOC DSM. Residual kriging neither gains accuracy nor costs calibration: it loses 0.014 R² against B1 (0.205 vs 0.219) and its PICP is indistinguishable (0.945 vs 0.944). An earlier version of this table reported the opposite on both counts — a +0.01 R² gain bought with a PICP of 0.82 — and that was an artefact: B2’s training residuals were formed from IN-SAMPLE forest predictions, which are too small by about 4x, so the kriged correction and its variance were both understated and B2’s intervals came out too narrow. With out-of-bag predictions the intervals are right, the PICP recovers, and the apparent accuracy gain disappears with it. The plain QRF is still the calibration champion, now on a wider margin in interval score rather than in PICP. The MoCo v1 embedding does not yet beat B1 on this dataset — v1 was trained for only 20 k InfoNCE steps (10% of the canonical MoCo v2 budget); v2 is in training, v1.3.2 will re-benchmark.

Reproduce with

Rscript data-raw/case_cerrado_prepare.R   # ~60 min, downloads ~2 GB
Rscript data-raw/case_cerrado_run.R       # ~3 min

or read the pre-computed .rds shipped at inst/extdata/case_cerrado_results.rds and rebuild every plot via vignette("case-cerrado-end-to-end").

Each vignette is written in the style of a short methods paper — abstract, numbered sections with LaTeX derivations, shared BibTeX bibliography (vignettes/references.bib).

Testing and continuous integration

  • 2 192 passing expectations across 601 test_that blocks in 92 test files (testthat), measured on aarch64-apple-darwin23, R 4.6.1. One expectation is skipped here, because its optional dependency is absent; every skip is an explicit skip_if_not_installed() gate.
  • Gated dependencies: torch, dagitty, bnlearn, dbarts, reticulate, terra, igraph.
  • R CMD check --as-cran: 2 NOTEs at commit 8e725b9. The per-item breakdown, including which items are package defects and which are artefacts of the checking machine, is in cran-comments.md; the log itself is committed at tools/status/check.log.
  • CI: GitHub Actions matrix on macos-latest / R release, windows-latest / R release, ubuntu-latest / R devel, ubuntu-latest / R release, ubuntu-latest / R oldrel-1, ubuntu-latest / R release. 1 of these 6 legs installs libtorch, so the torch-gated tests execute in CI rather than skipping.
  • These figures are generated by tools/status/patch-readme-metrics.R from a real test run and a real check log. Do not edit them by hand.
